title: FLUX.1 Kontext · conditioning
question: What happens to the reference while the output is sampled?
choices: It stays fixed as conditioning.
It is denoised with the target.
It becomes the target noise.
It is used only after decoding.
explanation: The reference provides context tokens while the target sequence evolves. See Architecture, §3 of the paper.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · time direction
question: With zₜ = (1−t)x + tε, which direction generates an image?
choices: t = 0 toward 1
t = 1 toward 0
Only t = 0.5
Time is the reference-image index.
explanation: t = 1 is noise and t = 0 is the clean target. Backward integration explains the minus sign in the toy Euler update.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · velocity
question: For x = 2 and ε = 10, what is the exact training velocity?
explanation: Differentiate (1−t)x + tε with respect to t: ε−x = 8. The sampling update goes backward in time.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · position
question: What does the 1 in reference position (1, h, w) mean?
choices: Noise level is maximal.
First denoising step.
The model has one channel.
It identifies the reference separately from target positions.
explanation: The virtual time coordinate separates image sequences. It is distinct from the flow noise time t.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · dev
question: Which statement matches the report’s dev recipe?
choices: LADD with the same joint task training as pro.
Guidance distillation into a 12B transformer, focused on image-to-image.
No model training ever takes place.
A demonstrated multiple-reference video model.
explanation: Section 3 distinguishes dev guidance distillation and editing-only training from pro’s flow training followed by LADD.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · metric
question: An editor returns the reference unchanged and gets a high face-similarity score. What follows?
choices: The edit succeeded.
Its text rendering is correct.
Identity similarity alone cannot establish instruction following.
All image quality metrics must be low.
explanation: An unchanged reference can preserve identity while ignoring the instruction. Evaluate preservation and the requested change together.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · benchmark
question: What does 1,026 refer to in KontextBench?
choices: Image–prompt pairs, derived from 108 base images.
Independent source photographs.
Editing categories.
Denoising steps.
explanation: Section 4.1 reports 1,026 pairs across five categories. Several instructions can reuse a base image.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · multi image
question: What is established about multiple reference images in this report?
choices: They are the focus of every experiment.
They are impossible with sequence concatenation.
They require identical image resolutions.
The formulation extends to them, but the report focuses on single-reference conditioning.
explanation: An architecture supporting an extension is different from evidence that the extension was trained and evaluated.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · limits
question: How should you describe multi-turn consistency?
choices: Unlimited edits without drift.
Reduced drift in reported comparisons, with failures still documented.
A pixel-preservation guarantee.
Evidence that distillation cannot cause artifacts.
explanation: Section 5 and Figure 15 show identity degradation, instruction failures, and artifacts after repeated edits.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · concat
question: Why can sequence concatenation handle different input/output grids?
choices: It makes the images have identical pixels.
It discards reference positions.
It appends separate token sequences rather than pairing channels at each matching location.
It removes attention.
explanation: Separate sequences can contain different numbers of spatial tokens. Position embeddings retain their spatial organization.

title: DiffAtlas · joint
question: What does DiffAtlas learn jointly?
choices: Images and their matching mask representations
Only masks conditioned on clean scans
A fixed atlas deformation for each patient
Text and images
explanation: It denoises image–mask pairs, learning their joint distribution. Inference then uses noisy image replacement to condition generation.

title: DiffAtlas · replacement
question: At inference, what is replaced at each time step?
choices: Both image and mask with fresh noise
Only the image part, with the appropriately noised patient scan
Only the mask, with the annotation
The network weights
explanation: Image channels are overwritten with the observed scan noised to the current level. The mask state carries progress forward.

title: DiffAtlas · noise
question: Why use a noisy patient scan instead of a clean scan at every step?
choices: To hide the patient from the model
To remove the need for annotated training data
To match the image corruption level expected at the current time
To update the model weights at test time
explanation: Training uses noisy paired states at each time. Replacement should match that corruption level.

title: DiffAtlas · sdf
question: What extra information does a signed distance field give?
choices: A guaranteed correct segmentation
Only the organ class name
The time until diffusion finishes
Distance to a boundary and which side a location is on
explanation: The field encodes graded geometry rather than just a discrete label. It encourages continuity but does not guarantee correctness.

title: DiffAtlas · number
question: With ᾱ = 0.64, image value 0.8, and noise 0.2, what is the noisy image value?

title: DiffAtlas · loss
question: What does the paper’s training loss compare?
choices: Predicted mask and patient age
Predicted noise and known added noise, across both image and mask
Two registration deformation fields
Only Dice scores from different datasets
explanation: Equation 6 trains noise prediction on the pair. The training loss changes weights; inference replacement changes the current sample state.

title: DiffAtlas · zero
question: What does zero-shot CT-to-MRI evaluation mean here?
choices: The model never sees any training data
MRI ground-truth masks are inserted during sampling
Source CT training is used without target MRI training
The target MRI scan is never shown to the model
explanation: The model has learned from labeled source data. Target scans guide inference, but target-modality training is absent.

title: DiffAtlas · ablation
question: Do the reported baseline comparisons isolate the benefit of the SDF alone?
choices: Yes, any higher Dice proves the SDF caused it
Yes, because SDF guarantees anatomy
Yes, because all diffusion methods are identical
No; a controlled component ablation is needed
explanation: Several design choices differ. The v1 comparisons support the tested system but do not isolate each component’s causal contribution.

title: REPA · teacher
question: What does the REPA teacher receive during training?
choices: The same clean image corresponding to the noisy latent.
Only the class label.
The model’s final generated image.
Fresh Gaussian noise unrelated to the example.
explanation: The frozen visual encoder supplies clean-image feature targets while the generator receives a corrupted latent.

title: REPA · gradient
question: Which parameters does the alignment branch directly train?
choices: The frozen VAE decoder.
The teacher encoder.
The projection and generator blocks upstream of its attachment.
Only generator blocks after the attachment.
explanation: Alignment gradients flow through the projection into the early generator; later blocks are trained by the generation loss.

title: REPA · cosine
question: A projected feature is multiplied by a positive factor of 10. What happens to its cosine similarity?
choices: It increases tenfold.
It stays the same, for nonzero vectors.
It becomes zero.
It must become negative.
explanation: Cosine divides the dot product by both vector lengths; a positive scale cancels.

title: REPA · loss
question: Velocity loss is 1, REPA loss is −0.8, and λ is 0.5. What is the combined loss?
explanation: The objective is 1 + 0.5 × (−0.8) = 0.6. Negative cosine is intentionally minimized.

title: REPA · inference
question: What extra REPA networks must be evaluated for each generated image?
choices: Both DINOv2 and the projection.
The teacher but not the projection.
Neither the teacher nor projection is needed.
Only the projection.
explanation: They provide training supervision; sampling retains the trained generator and VAE decoder.

title: REPA · speed
question: What does the 7M / 400K = 17.5 comparison directly establish?
choices: 17.5 times fewer training iterations at better reported unguided FID.
17.5 times fewer sampling steps.
17.5 times lower total compute including teacher pretraining.
17.5 times faster image decoding.
explanation: The table compares iteration budgets and FID, not wall-clock time or sampling cost.

title: REPA · depth
question: Depth 16 has better probe accuracy but worse FID than depth 8. What follows?
choices: Classification accuracy guarantees better generation.
More semantic probe accuracy need not improve generation quality.
REPA cannot improve generation.
The teacher must run during sampling.
explanation: Table 2 separates two goals: recognition-friendly representations and generation performance.

title: REPA · time
question: For zₜ = (1−t)z + tε, which sampling direction reaches data?
choices: 0 toward 1.
Keep t fixed.
Alternate 0 and 1.
1 toward 0.
explanation: At t=1 the state is noise; at t=0 it is data. A backward Euler ODE illustration subtracts a positive step times velocity.

title: Mean Flows · curvature
question: Why can generation curve despite straight training pairs?
choices: The marginal velocity averages possible pairs at each state.
Every training pair is secretly curved.
The VAE always rotates each step.
Only numerical errors cause curvature.
explanation: The changing conditional mean of pair velocities can induce curved marginal ODE trajectories even with exact fields.

title: Mean Flows · interval
question: Why does average velocity depend on destination time r?
choices: It selects a training image.
Different intervals can have different average velocities.
It counts transformer blocks.
It sets the random seed.
explanation: Average velocity summarizes a specified interval, so changing its destination changes the quantity being predicted.

title: Mean Flows · jvp
question: Which JVP tangent differentiates u(z, r, t) along the flow with fixed r?
explanation: The state moves with velocity v, destination r stays fixed, and current time increases at unit rate.

title: Mean Flows · detach
question: What does stopping the target gradient accomplish?
choices: It freezes the network forever.
It removes the JVP value from the target.
It makes the target identical at every update.
It avoids backpropagating through the target JVP during the weight update.
explanation: The target still uses the derivative and changes across updates; only its gradient contribution is detached.

title: Mean Flows · numbers
question: If v = 4, t − r = 0.5 and JVP = 2, what is the target?
explanation: The MeanFlow target is 4 − 0.5 × 2 = 3.

title: Mean Flows · diagonal
question: What happens to the training target when r = t?
choices: It divides by zero.
The correction vanishes, giving the Flow Matching target.
The entire loss is always zero.
It becomes the clean image.
explanation: The target formula multiplies the derivative by t − r, so diagonal samples use instantaneous velocity supervision.

title: Mean Flows · nfe
question: Why can guided MeanFlow sampling retain 1-NFE?
choices: The unconditional call is not counted.
Guidance is removed entirely.
The model learns the guided average field during training.
VAE decoding performs the second flow call.
explanation: Guidance enters the training target, allowing a single conditional average-velocity prediction at inference. VAE decoding is separate work.

title: Mean Flows · evidence
question: Which statement correctly describes the course Table 2 result of FID 2.20?
choices: It is the 1-NFE result.
It uses no pretrained VAE.
It proves universal superiority.
It uses 2-NFE with XL/2+ trained for 1,000 epochs.
explanation: The main 240-epoch XL/2 gets 3.43 at 1-NFE and 2.93 at 2-NFE. The 2.20 result also changes training and configuration.
